q: During the detailing of a reinforced concrete member, the designer must ensure that the reinforcement remains functional throughout the structure's service life, especially under exposure to moisture, chlorides, and elevated temperatures. Which primary function of concrete cover directly addresses these durability and safety requirements?
o: To protect the reinforcing steel from corrosion and fire by providing a physical barrier against environmental and thermal exposure
To increase the effective depth of the section and thereby enhance the member's flexural capacity under service loads
To reduce the risk of longitudinal bar buckling by increasing the stiffness of the concrete core surrounding the reinforcement
To improve the bond between steel and concrete by embedding the reinforcement deeper within the section
n: Concrete cover protects the steel from corrosion (moisture, chlorides) and from fire. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 420.6.1 (ACI 318-14, R20.6.1).

q: A reinforced concrete beam is designed with adequate concrete cover around its reinforcement. From an ARCHITECTURAL and building durability standpoint, what is the MOST important purpose of providing concrete cover?
o: To protect the reinforcement from corrosion and fire while maintaining the appearance and long-term durability of the structure
To maintain sufficient separation between reinforcement and formwork, ensuring proper placement, concrete consolidation, and quality of finish during construction.
To improve the long-term appearance of exposed concrete surfaces by minimizing staining, surface defects, and premature deterioration caused by environmental exposure.
To enhance the service life of the member by reducing maintenance requirements and preserving the integrity of the concrete envelope throughout the building's lifecycle.
n: Cover protects the bars from corrosion and fire, which keeps the structure durable and its appearance intact. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 420.6.1.

q: When using ready-mixed concrete from a central mixing plant and using truck mixers or truck agitators to transport it, the time elapsed from the time water is added to the mix until the concrete is deposited in place at the site shall not exceed how many minutes?
n: Ready-mixed concrete must be discharged within 90 minutes of adding water to the cement. Source: ASTM C94 (Ready-Mixed Concrete), Sec. 12.7; DPWH Item 405.

q: To maintain consistency and moderate workability, what should be the slump range in accordance with ASTM C143?
n: A slump of 50–100 mm (2–4 in.) gives moderate, consistent workability for most beams, columns and slabs. It is measured by ASTM C143. Source: ACI 211.1, Table 6.3.1; ASTM C143.

q: What is the recommended concrete slump for Mass Concrete?
n: Mass concrete uses a low slump of about 25–50 mm (1–2 in.) to limit water and heat of hydration. Source: ACI 211.1, Table 6.3.1 (mass concrete 1–3 in.).

q: Used to determine the integrity and quality of structural concrete
n: Ultrasonic pulse velocity reveals voids, cracks and uniformity, so it is used to assess the integrity and quality of concrete. Source: ASTM C597.

q: A non-destructive testing method to conveniently and rapidly determine the strength of concrete
n: The rebound (Schmidt) hammer is a quick, non-destructive test that estimates strength from surface hardness. Source: ASTM C805.

q: Which standard curing duration allows complete hydration of cement compounds, ensuring structural integrity, resistance to delayed microcracking, and optimal strength development, based on the reaction of tricalcium silicates and dicalcium silicate with water?
n: Concrete strength is specified and tested at 28 days, when most hydration of C3S and C2S has occurred. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, Ch. 9; NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 419.2 (f'c at 28 days).

q: Which kind of reinforcement cannot be found in slabs?
n: Slabs carry main, temperature, bent and longitudinal bars, but not vertical main bars. Those belong to columns and walls. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Secs. 407–408 (slab reinforcement).

q: Which is not a component of a Structural Plan?
n: The Site Development Plan belongs to the architectural set. Structural plans include general notes, foundation plans, and floor and roof framing plans. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule III, Sec. 302 (structural and architectural documents).

q: According to the NSCP, the spacing of lateral ties in reinforced concrete columns shall not exceed ___ times the diameter of the smallest longitudinal bar, 48 times the tie bar diameter, or the least lateral dimension of the column.
n: Tie spacing may not exceed 16 longitudinal bar diameters, 48 tie bar diameters, or the least column dimension. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 425.7.2.1.

q: During a post-earthquake forensic assessment of a mid-rise RC building, the engineer observes that several columns developed diagonal shear cracks near the ends, but the core concrete remained largely intact and the longitudinal bars did not exhibit outward buckling. The transverse reinforcement in these regions consisted of closely spaced closed ties with 135° hooks. while mid-height ties were spaced farther apart. Which structural mechanism MOST directly explains why the column ends maintained integrity despite severe cyclic loading?
o: The increased axial load capacity provided by the transverse reinforcement in the plastic hinge region
The prevention of longitudinal bar buckling and the confinement of core concrete provided by closely spaced lateral ties in the plastic hinge zone
The reduction of flexural tension demand in the longitudinal bars due to confinement effects
The redistribution of bending moments from the column ends to the mid-height due to tie spacing variation
n: Closely spaced closed ties with 135° hooks in the plastic-hinge zone confine the core and stop the longitudinal bars from buckling. That is why the column ends stayed intact. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 418.7.5.

q: A reinforced concrete beam supporting a masonry wall suddenly develops diagonal cracks near its supports. During inspection, the cracks are found to run diagonally upward toward the point of loading, and the beam exhibits little warning before failure. Investigation reveals that the transverse reinforcement was insufficient for the applied load. What type of failure most likely occurred?
o: Flexural Failure, because the tension reinforcement at midspan was insufficient to resist bending stresses.
Torsional Failure, because twisting stresses developed within the member and exceeded its resistance to rotation.
Shear Failure, because diagonal tension stresses exceeded the beam's shear- resisting capacity near the supports
Buckling Failure, because the compression zone of the beam became laterally unstable under loading.
n: Diagonal cracks near the supports, running toward the load and failing with little warning, mean a shear (diagonal tension) failure from too few stirrups. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 422.5; Nilson, Design of Concrete Structures, Ch. 4.

q: During a column reinforcement inspection, the engineer notes that the transverse reinforcement consists of closed rectangular bars placed at regular intervals, enclosing all longitudinal bars and anchored with proper hooks. These bars are spaced more closely near the column ends and more widely at mid-height. Which reinforcement element is being described?
n: Closed transverse bars enclosing a column's longitudinal bars are lateral ties. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 425.7.2.

q: During a beam reinforcement inspection, the engineer observes transverse reinforcement consisting of closed rectangular bars that wrap completely around all longitudinal: tension and compression bars. These transverse bars are spaced tightly near the supports, where diagonal cracking is expected, and more widely at midspan. Their primary role is to resist diagonal tension and prevent shear failure. Which reinforcement element is being described?
n: In beams, closed transverse bars that resist diagonal tension and shear are stirrups. They are closer near the supports. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 409.7.6 and Sec. 422.5.

q: What is the distance from the clear face of the supporting column or joint to the first stirrup?
n: The first hoop or stirrup is placed no more than 50 mm from the face of the supporting member. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 418.6.4.4.

q: What is the minimum bend diameter for Stirrups, Ties and Hoops?
n: Stirrups, ties and hoops of 16 mm diameter and smaller need a minimum inside bend diameter of 4db. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Table 425.3.2.

q: What is the minimum bend diameter for deformed bars in tension?
n: Deformed bars 10–25 mm in diameter need a minimum bend diameter of 6db for standard hooks. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Table 425.3.1.

q: Which term defines the equivalent span of a beam, adjusted based on boundary conditions and support restraint, used in buckling and deflection calculations to determine its true structural behavior under loading?
n: Effective length (KL) is the equivalent pinned length adjusted for end restraint. It is used in buckling and deflection calculations. Source: AISC 360-16, Appendix 7; Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 13.

q: Which structural steel section is engineered for maximum flexural performance, featuring parallel, non-tapered flanges with optimized width-to-depth ratio, ensuring superior lateral stability, reduced flange buckling and improved moment distribution in high-load applications?
n: Wide-flange (W) sections have parallel, untapered flanges and efficient proportions for bending. Standard I-beams (S) have tapered flanges. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, 15th ed., Part 1.

q: In structural steel design, what is the primary function of a base plate in a steel column, ensuring proper load transfer, stability and foundation integration?
o: Acting as an anchoring surface to transfer column loads efficiently to the foundation, reducing bearing stresses and preventing localized failure
Eliminating the need for anchor bolts by offering direct load transmission through frictional contact alone
Serving as a decorative attachment to improve architectural aesthetics rather than performing a structural function
Providing a rigid moment connection to enhance lateral load resistance
n: A base plate spreads the column load over a larger area of concrete, lowering bearing stress. It is anchored to the foundation with anchor rods. Source: AISC Design Guide 1 (Base Plate and Anchor Rod Design).

q: Which part of an I-beam structural steel section resists shear forces?
n: In an I-section, the web resists shear. The flanges resist bending. Source: Salmon & Johnson, Steel Structures, Ch. 7.

q: If an I-beam structural steel section has equal or nearly equal width and depth, it is more suited for use as a?
n: An I-shape with roughly equal width and depth (H or column section) has similar stiffness about both axes, so it suits columns. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, 15th ed., Part 1 (W-shapes used as columns).

q: In steel construction, which section is most commonly used as a beam due to its high bending strength, symmetrical flange geometry, and efficient load distribution—typically designated as W-sections under AISC standards?
n: Wide-flange (W) sections are the standard steel beams under AISC designations. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, 15th ed., Part 1.

q: In steel roof truss construction, which steel section is most commonly used for top chords, bottom chords, and web members due to its ease of fabrication, suitability for triangulated configurations, and cost efficiency?
n: Light roof trusses are usually made of single or double angles for chords and webs. Angles are easy to fabricate and economical. Source: Salmon & Johnson, Steel Structures (truss members).

q: What is the item W4x13 stand for in structural steel design?
o: Steel flange, weighing 4 pounds and 13 inches high
W section, 4 inches wide and 13 inches high
Wide flange, 4 inches high and weighing 13 pounds per foot
W flange, 4 inches high and 13 inches wide
n: In W4x13, 4 is the nominal depth in inches and 13 is the weight in pounds per linear foot. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, 15th ed., Part 1 (Dimensions and Properties).

q: In the steel beam designation W40x60, what does the number "60" represent?
n: In W40x60, the second number (60) is the weight in lb/ft. The 40 is the nominal depth in inches. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, 15th ed., Part 1.

q: Which structural steel beam is best for resisting twisting and warping under torsional loading?
n: Closed box sections resist torsion and warping far better than open I- or W-shapes. Source: Salmon & Johnson, Steel Structures, Ch. 8 (Torsion).

q: Which directly supports the load from the roof?
n: Purlins directly support the roof covering and carry its load to the rafters or trusses. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (roof framing).

q: What structural member typically supports the roof covering between adjacent frames or trusses in a steel roof system?
o: Girder, because it serves as a primary horizontal member that supports secondary framing elements.
Joist, because it functions as a closely spaced framing member that supports floors and roofs.
Rafters, because they transfer roof loads to the main structural frame and often support purlins.
Purlins, because they span between frames or trusses and directly support the roof sheeting or decking.
n: Purlins span between frames or trusses and directly support the roof sheeting or decking. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: A structural system comprising of straight members that acts as either tension or compression intended to carry the roof.
n: A truss is a triangulated system of straight members acting in tension or compression, commonly used to carry roofs. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (trusses).

q: Most common purlin section
n: Cold-formed C-purlins are the most common purlin section in local light-gauge steel roofing. Z-purlins are used where laps are needed. Source: AISI S100 (cold-formed steel); local light-gauge steel practice.

q: Which is not a Steel Section?
n: SHS (square hollow section), CHS (circular hollow section) and RHS (rectangular hollow section) are standard steel sections. "HHS" is not. Source: ASTM A500 / EN 10219 hollow section designations.

q: In steel construction, what is the primary reason for specifying minimum bolt spacing in beam-to-beam or beam-to-column connections?
o: To reduce the cost of fabrication
To prevent stress concentration and ensure proper load distribution
To allow for future expansion of the connection
n: Minimum bolt spacing (about 3d, at least 2⅔d) prevents stress concentration and tear-out between holes, so load is shared properly. Source: AISC 360-16, Sec. J3.3.

q: In timber framing, what do you call a stiff vertical structural member that supports beams and transfers loads to the foundation?
n: A post is a stiff vertical timber member that supports beams and carries loads down to the foundation. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood post-and-beam framing).

q: Which horizontal framing member is anchored to the top of a foundation wall and serves as the base for wall construction?
n: A sill plate is anchored to the top of the foundation wall and is the base of the wall framing. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood light framing).

q: Studs shall have full bearing on a plate or sill not less than thick having a width not less than that of the wall studs.
n: Studs must bear fully on a plate or sill at least 50 mm thick and no narrower than the studs. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII (Group A dwellings), Wood Construction; NSCP 2015, Ch. 6.

q: What is the minimum elevation requirement for a sill plate above finished grade, considering moisture 'exposure and termite infestation risk?
o: Directly on soil with termite-resistant coating
At least 150 mm (6 inches) above finished grade
Flush with grade to maximize structural contact
n: Wood sill plates must be at least 150 mm (6 in.) above finished grade to limit moisture and termite exposure. Source: IRC R317.1 (protection of wood against decay); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What do you call the vertical distance between the finished floor level (FFL) and the underside of a beam soffit?
n: Clear height is the vertical distance from the finished floor to the underside (soffit) of a beam. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NBC IRR, Rule VIII, Sec. 805 (headroom clearance).

q: Which structural system is most suitable for covering large-span roofs with complex geometry and minimal internal supports, such as those found in stadiums, airports, and atriums?
n: Space frames, three-dimensional triangulated grids, cover large spans and complex geometries with few interior supports, as in stadiums, airports and atriums. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (space frames); Schodek, Structures.

q: What is the primary use of a space frame in architectural and structural design?
o: To resist lateral Joads in retaining walls
To span large areas with minimal internal supports
To provide flexible partition ing in interiors
To support deep foundations in soft soil
n: A space frame is used to span large areas with minimal internal supports. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Schodek, Structures.

q: A structural system derives its stability primarily from members carrying tension rather than compression or bending. It is commonly used in stadiums, airport terminals, and exhibition pavilions where large column-free spaces and lightweight roofs are desired. What structural system is being described?
o: Space Frame, because its three-dimensional configuration efficiently distributes loads through interconnected compression and tension members.
Tensile Structure, because its stability is achieved primarily through membranes, cables, or other elements that remain in tension.
Shell Structure, because its curved geometry enables loads to be transferred through membrane stresses within the surface.
Steel Truss, because its triangulated arrangement permits long spans while utilizing both tension and compression members.
n: A tensile structure gets its stability from membranes or cables in tension. It is used for light, column-free roofs. Source: Schodek, Structures (tension structures).

q: The widespread use of tensile structures for large-span roofs is often limited by which factor that most directly affects their structural behavior and long-term performance?
o: Rain Load, because ponding water can alter membrane geometry and increase localized loading.
Prestressing Requirements, because inadequate tensioning can lead to excessive deformation arid toss of structural stability. PFIRG UTILITIES
High-Velocity Wind, because tensile structures are lightweight and highly sensitive to uplift, flutter, and aerodynamic instability.
Material Durability, because membrane materials may degrade over time due to ultraviolet exposure and environmental effects.
n: Tensile roofs are light and highly sensitive to wind: uplift, flutter and aerodynamic instability. Wind therefore governs their design and limits their use. Source: Schodek, Structures; ASCE 55 (Tensile Membrane Structures).
